issues.legal_issue: A temple’s public or private character depends on the intended beneficiaries and the evidence of dedication and public worship, and the evidence did not establish a hereditary trusteeship in the claimant’s family.
material_facts: The official inam-register entries identified the deity as the owner or pattadar of the temple lands and described the endowment as being for the religious institution and the temple’s maintenance.
The entries recorded persons outside the claimant’s family as managers of the temple or its lands.
Witnesses described members of the public, including people from neighbouring villages, as having access to the temple to worship, sometimes using a key left available when the claimant was absent.

The family partition deed, will and register prepared by the claimant’s father did not establish that the family’s claimed hereditary management had been acted upon; the claimed fact that the temple was in the claimant’s residence was not supported by the evidence.
The claimant’s father had earlier sought a determination that the temple was private, but that claim was rejected, and he was later appointed as a trustee for a limited term.
issues.conclusion: The temple was public, not private, and the claimant failed to establish that he was its hereditary trustee.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 9(12) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926, a public temple is distinguished from a private one by the nature of the beneficiaries and the founder’s intention: an endowment for specified individuals is private, while one for the general body of worshippers is public. Public access alone does not necessarily make a temple public, but public use without interference is cogent evidence of public dedication when the endowment is in favour of the idol (Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar; Babu Bhagwan Gir v. Gir Har Saroon). In the relevant former Madras Presidency region, the court applied the presumption that temples and their endowments are public religious trusts, rebuttable by affirmative and compelling evidence (Mundancheri Koman v. Achutan Nair; T.V. Mahalinga Iyer v. State of Madras). Inam-register entries are important evidence of the history and tenure of property (Arunachellam Chetty v. Venkatachalapathi Guruswamigal; Narayan Bhagwantrao Gosavi Balajiwale v. Gopal Vinayah Gosavi), though they must be read with the other recorded circumstances (The Poohari Fakir Sadavarthy of Bondilipuram v. Commissioner, Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments).

rule.if: public_or_private_temple_determination and dedication_to_deity_shown_by_official_records and (public_worship_without_interference or public_temple_presumption_applies) and family_claim_not_supported_by_conduct and other_managers_recorded

predicates.public_or_private_temple_determination: The proceeding required the court to determine whether a place of worship was a public or private temple.
predicates.dedication_to_deity_shown_by_official_re: Official records identified the deity as owner or pattadar of the property and recorded the property as dedicated for the religious institution or its maintenance.
predicates.public_worship_without_interference: Members of the public were able to enter or use the temple to worship without interference.
predicates.public_temple_presumption_applies: The temple was in a region where the court applied an initial presumption that temples and their endowments were public religious trusts.
predicates.family_claim_not_supported_by_conduct: The claimant’s family documents asserting hereditary management were not supported by evidence that the family had acted in accordance with those assertions.
predicates.other_managers_recorded: Official records identified persons outside the claimant’s family as managers of the temple or its property.

issues.definition: When a temple-character proceeding shows dedication to the deity, public access or an applicable presumption of public character, and the claimed family succession is unsupported while other managers are recorded, the temple is public and hereditary trusteeship in the claimant is not established.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings in an appeal by special leave are not open to further scrutiny unless they suffer from an error of law.
material_facts: Both the trial court and the High Court found that the temple was public and that the claimant had not established hereditary trusteeship.
The Supreme Court considered the claimant’s challenges to those findings and found no error of law warranting interference.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent findings were upheld and were not reopened on the facts.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, a concurrent finding of fact is not open to further scrutiny by the Supreme Court in an appeal by special leave unless it suffers from an error of law (Narayan Bhagwantrao Gosavi Balajiwale v. Gopal Vinayah Gosavi).

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter came before the Supreme Court as an appeal by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The courts below reached the same findings on the material facts.
predicates.no_error_of_law_found: The Supreme Court found no error of law in those concurrent findings.

issues.definition: When an appeal by special leave challenges concurrent factual findings and the Supreme Court finds no error of law, those findings are not reopened.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant cannot acquire property of a religious institution by prescription if the claimed title had not vested before the statutory cutoff applicable to the institution’s region.
material_facts: The claimant asserted adverse possession of the temple lands after his father’s death in 1946.
The father had been appointed a trustee, and the claimant did not assert that his father’s possession was adverse to the trust.
Even assuming the claimant’s possession became adverse in 1946, the claimed title had not been acquired by prescription before the relevant statutory cutoff of September 30, 1951.
The temple was in the Andhra area to which section 103 of the 1966 Act applied.
issues.conclusion: The claimant had not acquired title to the temple lands by adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: Section 94 of the 1951 Act and section 103 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, prevent limitation law from vesting property of a religious institution in a person unless the right had vested before the applicable statutory cutoff. For the Andhra area, section 103 makes September 30, 1951 the relevant date for determining whether title by prescription had been acquired.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim_against_religio: A claimant seeks title by adverse possession to property held for a religious institution.
predicates.property_in_region_with_statutory_cutoff: The property is in a region for which a statutory cutoff governs whether limitation can vest religious-institution property in a claimant.
predicates.adverse_possession_started_after_trustee: The claimant’s alleged adverse possession began only after the prior holder’s possession as trustee ended.
predicates.prescriptive_title_not_completed_by_cuto: The claimant had not completed the requirements for prescriptive title before the applicable statutory cutoff.

issues.definition: If a claimant seeks adverse possession of religious-institution property in a region with a statutory cutoff, and prescriptive title was not completed by that cutoff, title is not acquired by adverse possession.

issues.legal_issue: Property recorded as completely dedicated to a deity does not retain its private and secular character merely because the claimant asserts that only part of the property was dedicated.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a family partition deed to argue that income remaining after temple expenses was for the family’s benefit and that the dedication was therefore partial.
The inam-register entries showed that the lands were property of the deity and were granted for the maintenance of the temple.
The court had rejected the claimant’s case founded on the family document and accepted the official entries as showing complete dedication.
issues.conclusion: The property was completely dedicated to the deity and did not retain a private or secular character through partial dedication.
issues.legal_principle: The distinction between complete and partial dedication may affect whether property retains its private and secular character; however, the court found on the evidence that the property was completely dedicated to the deity. The court referred to S. Shanmugam Pillai v. K. Shanmugam Pillai in addressing the partial-dedication contention.

predicates.partial_dedication_claim: A party asserts that only part of property was dedicated to a religious purpose and that the property otherwise remained private.
predicates.official_records_show_complete_dedicatio: Official records identify the property as belonging to the deity and dedicated for the maintenance of the religious institution.

issues.definition: When a partial-dedication claim is contradicted by official records showing complete dedication to the deity, the property is treated as fully dedicated to the deity.
